subject: math
title: A-Math trigonometry: identities, compound angles and the R-formula

slides.heading: A-Math trigonometry: identities, compound angles and the R-formula
bullets: Identities, compound angles and the R-formula: one coherent trigonometry toolkit
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in: today we ground the two seed identities on the unit circle, compute sin 75 degrees exactly, merge two waves with the R-formula, and expose the splitting trap.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Use sin squared plus cos squared equals one and tan equals sin over cos
Compute sin 75 degrees exactly and rewrite 3 cos x + 4 sin x in R-form
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the cosine splitting trap.

slides.heading: Can you find sin 75 degrees exactly?
bullets: 75 degrees is not on the basic table - but 45 plus 30 is
And can two separate waves really be one single cosine?
slides.notes: Ask the class to vote: can sin 75 degrees be found exactly without a calculator? Take answers, then promise the compound angle formula does it in four familiar values.

slides.heading: Three tools for A-Math trigonometry
bullets: The seed identities: sin squared plus cos squared equals one, and tan is sin over cos
Compound angle formulae expand sin(A + B) and cos(A + B) into familiar values
The R-formula rewrites a cos x + b sin x as one cosine, R cos(x - alpha)
slides.notes: Say this slowly: identities simplify, compound formulae expand sums of angles, and the R-formula merges two waves into one so max, min and period are obvious.

slides.heading: The two seed identities, on the unit circle
bullets: On the unit circle the legs are cos theta and sin theta with hypotenuse 1
So sin squared plus cos squared equals one, and tan is sin over cos
slides.notes: Point at the animation: the probe travels the unit circle, the legs reshape, but the hypotenuse stays 1 - that is why the identity always holds.

slides.heading: Compound angles: computing sin 75 degrees
bullets: sin 75 degrees is sin(45 + 30) = sin 45 cos 30 + cos 45 sin 30
The four values multiply out to (root 6 + root 2) over 4, about 0.966
slides.notes: Follow the four familiar values as they fly into their slots: root 2 over 2 times root 3 over 2 plus root 2 over 2 times one half.

slides.heading: The R-formula: one wobble, not two
bullets: For 3 cos x + 4 sin x, R is 5 from the 3-4-5 triangle and alpha is 53.1 degrees
So 3 cos x + 4 sin x = 5 cos(x - 53.1 degrees), with max 5 and min -5
slides.notes: Watch the two waves merge into one cosine of amplitude 5: once it is a single wave, the maximum, minimum and period are immediate.

slides.heading: Misconception: cos(A + B) does not split
bullets: cos 60 degrees is 0.5, but cos 30 + cos 30 is about 1.73
The trap claim is: cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B.
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud: cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B. The fix is: Use cos A cos B - sin A sin B: cos 60 is 0.5 but cos 30 + cos 30 is about 1.73.

slides.heading: Worked example: sin 75 degrees exactly
bullets: Step 1: write 75 as 45 + 30 and expand sin(45 + 30)
Step 2: substitute the four known values to get (root 6 + root 2) over 4
slides.notes: Talk through it slowly: sin 45 cos 30 plus cos 45 sin 30, then root 6 plus root 2 over 4, about 0.966 - check it against a calculator value for sin 75.

slides.heading: Your turn: expand, merge, then check the trap
bullets: Compute sin 75 degrees from the compound formula and rewrite 3 cos x + 4 sin x in R-form
Careful - a classmate claims: cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B. Explain why that fails using cos 60 degrees
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call: listen for the trap - cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B. The fix is: Use cos A cos B - sin A sin B: cos 60 is 0.5 but cos 30 + cos 30 is about 1.73.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: On your own: state the exact value of sin 75 degrees
Watch out for the trap one last time: cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B. Say what cos(A + B) really expands to
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - cos(A + B) = cos A + cos B. - and the fix: Use cos A cos B - sin A sin B: cos 60 is 0.5 but cos 30 + cos 30 is about 1.73. Collect the tickets as they leave.
